banning one financial product does not necessarily eliminate the demand for speculation. It may simply push that demand into another form
one that is farther away, more complicated, and less visible. But everything we've discussed does not mean that South Koreans are
inherently greedy or obsessed with getting rich quickly. When an entire system puts pressure on people every day, choices that look
irrational to outsiders can make perfect sense to the people facing those pressures. Imagine you're a 28-year-old South Korean. Your job
isn't stable. Your contract gets renewed one year at a time, and you have no idea what the future holds. Meanwhile
housing prices are so high that you have no idea when you'll ever be able to afford a home. Every
day, you open your phone and see the stock market rising. People are constantly showing off their profits. Stories about ordinary
people becoming rich are everywhere. In those circumstances, staying on the sidelines is not easy. The scariest thing is not margin
trading itself. It's the reasons people turn to margin trading in the first place. If a generation grows up feeling that
working hard may not be enough to live comfortably, that saving for years may still not buy them a decent home
and that following the old rules will only leave them further behind, then the search for riskier options becomes almost inevitable
It isn't necessarily greed. It's a sense of helplessness, a fear of falling behind, and a belief that if you don't
speed up, you'll never catch up. And here's the irony: in the short term, the market often rewards exactly that way
of thinking. Every time the market falls and then rebounds, leveraged investors feel vindicated. They look at the profits in their
accounts and think, 'See? I was right! I'm amazing at investing. Next time, I should go even bigger.' This is one
of the market's most dangerous traps: it makes people confuse luck with skill. Winning once doesn't make you a stock-market genius
It may simply mean that you happened to be in the right place during favorable market conditions. One or two successful
trades can feel great. But it may only take a few bad ones to wipe out those gains. The debt remains
